  "text": "By morning Tobias had worn a pale place in the church door with his sleeve. He had sat against it all night. When the woman who kept the keys arrived, he stood and let her pass without saying why he was there.

From the churchyard he could see Maren's roof. Nothing else of the house showed above the dune.

He went by the road.

The eleven posts stood straight. He kept his hands in his pockets as he passed them. At the porch he found the lantern lying on its side. The glass was whole. A small snail had fastened itself to the handle.

He knocked with one knuckle.

The latch lifted when he tried it. Inside, the front room was cold and smelled of old ashes. The lamp stood unlit on the sill. He touched its chimney, then wiped his finger on his coat.

Her father's rug lay square with the boards. Tobias remembered helping carry it in, years ago, bent beneath the roll while Maren's mother told them not to scrape the door.

He called Maren once.

Before leaving, he set the lantern upright on the porch. He shut the door and pressed it until the latch caught.

At the last post he stopped. Through the front window he could see the back of the lamp, its chipped base turned toward him.

He had seen the chip from inside.

He waited a little, as though someone might come to the window and put it right.",

  "text": "In the weeks afterward, Tobias took the inland road. It added half an hour to his walk, and when anyone remarked on it he said the sand had got too deep.

No one asked him to fetch anything from the house.

Once, at the grocer's, he heard Maren's name spoken in the next aisle. He stood holding a paper bag until the bottom softened against his palm. Then he put it down and went out without what he had come for.

The woman who kept the church keys brought him a coat she had found beneath a pew. It was not his. He thanked her before he understood what she was holding, and afterward could not think how to give it back.

He hung it behind his kitchen door.

By November the dune grass had flattened. From the churchyard more of the house was visible: the upper window, a strip of wall, the dark edge of the porch. The eleven posts had disappeared into the grass.

One afternoon he went as far as the first of them. He had brought oil in a small tin, though he had not decided what he meant to do with it.

The lantern stood where he had left it. Its handle was bare.

He put the tin beside it and turned away.

At home he found the borrowed coat fallen from its peg. He picked it up, brushed the collar, and hung it again.

For the rest of the winter he used the other door.",

  "text": "In March the other door began to stick. Tobias lifted it by the handle each morning until the lower hinge pulled loose. The carpenter said it would be simpler to use the kitchen while he worked.

Tobias waited in the garden.

Through the window he could see the carpenter moving between the rooms. Once the man stopped beside the coat. He touched a sleeve, perhaps only to move it out of his way, then went on with his measuring.

When the work was finished, Tobias paid him at the gate.

There were pale shavings on the floor. He swept them into a pan and carried them outside. One had caught in the coat's cuff. He left it there.

The woman with the church keys died before Easter. Her daughter came to collect things people had borrowed: a ladder, cake tins, the long table used for sales. Tobias told her about the coat.

She said her mother had often brought home clothes left in the church.

‘Someone may still ask for it,’ she said.

He nodded. She wrote nothing down.

That evening he opened the kitchen door. It took some pressure; the hem was caught beneath it. He freed the cloth without looking into the pockets and folded the coat across a chair.

For several days he passed the empty peg with his eyes lowered.

Then he hung his own coat there.

When he needed it again, he stood in the kitchen a long time. Outside, the repaired door swung easily in the wind, touching its latch and falling back.",
